blocks.title: Pauli's exclusion principle
blocks.text: No two electrons in an atom can have the same values for all four quantum numbers; or, two electrons in an orbital will always have opposite spins.

In the first shell of a helium atom there are two electrons, both in the 1s orbital. By the concept of quantum numbers and Pauli's principle their quantum numbers are those of the table: the same n, l and m, but different values of s, so their spins are in opposite directions.

blocks.caption: Quantum numbers of the two electrons in one orbital (Table 2.6 as printed)

blocks.prompt: Could a third electron enter helium's 1s orbital? Use the principle to answer.
blocks.explanation: No. Any third electron in 1s would have n = 1, l = 0 and m = 0, and its spin would have to be +1/2 or -1/2, which would repeat all four quantum numbers of one of the two electrons already there. The principle forbids this, so the orbital is full with two.

items: Pauli: no two electrons in an atom share all four quantum numbers, so an orbital holds at most two electrons, with opposite spins (helium's 1s pair differs only in s).
